title: "Papa Jack" Laine, Mrs. "Papa Jack" Laine and Johnny Wiggs Interview, 1959-02-27

blocks.x: . The time they play in all that jazz stuff, there's too much breaks in it. Let me see. You know what I mean, Johnny? Yeah. It's not the right time at all at all. Yeah. I'm going to move your chair up. Yeah, that's... That sounded like... Beautiful, beautiful. That sounded like the old-time bands, didn't it? Don't miss it. Don't miss it. It was a lot of fun to play in those days. How come the drum beat came back to you so quickly? It's just... It was just natural that the drum beat came back to you, huh? No, Johnny, I can't use this leg at all on traps. No more. I'll make a fumble. I might get... For a while, you understand? Then... Yeah, but your beat, I mean... Oh, the beat. The cymbal beat. Oh, the cymbal beat. It came right back to your... You hadn't touched a drum... That's natural. You hadn't touched a drum in 40 years, huh? Easy. And the beat, the cymbal beat came right back to your knees, huh? That syncopated cymbal beat, huh? Yeah. It was very interesting. The minute I heard it, I got a kick out of it. Yeah, this is... I don't know... Johnny, I played a mighty fine trap drum. Yeah. If I do say it for myself. I can tell that. I can tell that. I played a mighty fine trap drum. I can tell that by your bass drum playing. Yes, I bet you did too. Yeah. I played a mighty fine trap drum. Yeah. If I could have played out to it, as well as I played trap drum, I'd have been a good musician. Yeah. Well, you know, one of the hardest things to find in a band is a good trap drummer. Johnny, believe me or not, one time ago I played for a bunch that Shillin was in it. Half a Shillin was in it. And he was way... Well, I guess he must have been about... Put me in a block. Above me. You understand? And I don't know now anymore, I can't remember whether he was in a band or what it was. But anyhow, we stopped for a rest on the road. And he come back and he says, I knew just who was playing that bass drum. Happy Shillin says. He says, I know just who was on that bass drum, he says. The minute he says I got in the ranks and started, he says, I know just who was on that bass drum. I guess he'd around. You know, you see, Johnny Fisher started, you know, he started, he had a pretty good band too. You know? Oh, hey. And, yeah. I had to cancel some of my drums, some of my jobs. That is not my jobs, but playing in my jobs, you understand? To play with the Fisher. He offered me any kind of money to go with him to play, you understand? So, I played a couple of, well, I had Rag Baby Stevens, I had Diddy Stevens, and I had Ernest Stevens. They're mighty good drum players, you know. I had them all the time to fill out. I went with Fisher, and I had his band up all around. And them guys shoved his chest out. Now, that's funny. Of course, everybody would praise themselves. I know that. Praise, don't go with me. But I do say, if it is myself, I kept them in time. Well, you can tell by the beat on that record. Yes, you can. And just imagine, you know, we didn't know what was going to happen after 40 years for you to sit down and play band strong. We didn't know what was going to happen, you know. So, you can imagine our delight and surprise. Get that scrapbook one. When we heard that beat. Yes. And that's the same kind of beat you used to play. I know that. It is. Because you did it naturally. It is. The same beat at the same time. The band must have sounded like the band you used to play with. Exactly. Because you seemed to fall in with it so easily. Exactly. Now, they had a pretty good swell drum player. Was in the 3rd Battalion.
What do you want to get out? What do you want to get?
I want to show John a little more of that last picture I took on that trap drum.
Oh, that one back on here.
Yeah.
Yeah. That ain't too long ago. Oh, it's about. Oh, yes. That was in the Times-Picayune. Yeah. You were 66 then and he's 85 now. Yeah.

It's been a long time ago. It's been a long time ago. They come and got me to take the picture, Johnny, you know? Yeah. Uh-huh. So, the Finnish Italian, they told this fella that he had no more business to be major in that band. And so, after they heard me, I understand, playing one thing or another, I went up there one fine night with a couple of the boys and I started to play with them, you understand? Jesus, they found it mighty different between before and when I was playing. Yeah. So, Major Violet come to me, you know, and he says to me, young man, he says, how would you like to be major in this band, take this band over? Oh, I said, Major Violet, I said, you got that man over there? I said, that wouldn't be right. He says, well, he said, I'll tell you.
Oh, you got to see that.

There's 35 or 36 men in this band here, he said, and they're all leaning to you. I said, I just said, well, I'll tell you this. He said, they want you. So, anyhow, I took over. You know, they all got on me, I took over. And, brother, when I got on the street with the military band, they played, they played one chorus and a voice, you know, one chorus and I'd follow in after. They'd stop. My band would then fill out. See? Then they'd start a game and I'd fill out, they'd start a game. It was that wonderful that I couldn't believe it myself. The marches that we played. Yeah. I couldn't believe it myself. Then I arranged, there was only bugles in it, that's all, just bugles. And I raised the band so that I got five or six picaloos in it. And, brother, that went to town. Went to town. You know them bugles and picaloos? They went to town. And I had pretty good drum players, mighty good drum players. Well, I practiced them with them, you know. That would show them the right beats and all that sort of stuff. Yeah. Cut them down fine. When we went on the street, brother, I had no war of it. Had no war of it. All I had to do was to blow my whistle and make it right in land. And go ahead. Now, that underarm march. Jesus, that was the beautifulest thing ever you heard in your life. Well, they'd play one voice in the chorus. You understand? Right after they'd play the first voice and the first chorus, we'd fall in the second. See? Then after we fall in the second, they'd pick up after and go into the third mine up to march. It was wonderful, John. It was wonderful. Can imagine. Oh, brother, wonderful. Major Bean used to, oh boy, used to give me anything that I want in that place. Anything at all that I want. I want to fix this. I want to fix that. Anything. Go ahead and have it done. Send me the bill. You had complete charge of the band, huh? Yeah. And Major Y.R. Violet, there were gentlemen, the two of them. Fine men. Fine men. I stayed in there until they went to ship us over, over to, uh, that was doing the Spanish and American war I'm speaking about now. They were going to take us over. And the Armistice was coming for days before they said this over.
That's the picture. I didn't know where it was, really.
Boy, boy.

But Georgie, oh, and that's all I had. He said, well, I don't want to take it away from you. Well, he said, I'll tell you what you do. Get Papa to try, you can get a copy. I said, yeah. So is Merritt on here?

His daddy came to hear us that afternoon. We played over in Gretna.
Oh yeah, yeah.

Yeah, he come here every time they came here. Every time George would come in town, he came with them, you know, and all. And that's when they give Popper the record. You remember that, Johnny.

yeah,

He's the one came down that morning early. He said, I got a surprise for you. He says, Mama, he said, guess what? He said, you're going to have a lot of company. I said, yeah. He said, yeah. George is in town, and Abby and Merritt and their wives and all is coming in. He said, with George. He said, He said, with George. He said,
it was a surprise,

too. I mean. I could never think, you know, with George. That poor George, he cried, he cried on my shoulder like a baby. Oh, I love him. I tell you the truth. I love him. He was my baby. He was my baby. He sure was my baby. All the time.
We had a nice place. I lived in a beautiful place. Yeah, I love George. He was so nice. Nice step going up there. And I had some cops up in there. All them kids used to come up there and flop
up there. Johnny Lala too. He used to play cornet too.
Johnny Lala was a good friend of mine. I used to play with him in Brownlee's band. Yeah,

he's nice. He's a wonderful fellow. He's a good boy. He used to sleep at our house when he had to go on jobs like that. And they was afraid they wouldn't get up because he worked late at the market. He would take

sleep than they had upstairs you know. And they had cots up there. They were sleeping. Yeah. Gentlemen that fellow used to raise more Santa power at night and keep pillaging for them. Fetish scattered off.

Oh they was terrible. Especially that Abby and Georgie. Yeah. You wouldn't imagine the mischief that Abby can brew. That Abby is a case. I'm telling you he's a case. I don't know if you remember I'll see Lunes Yellow Lunes it was a couple
of them.

They all had supper before they go to play music one night at my house on Polk Street. Abby was there in Georgie. And right on the windowsill by the table I had a little vine like that of tablets for the bowels. Oh little little bit of things. What did Abby do but yellow? He mixed it in yellow's food.
The

man had such cranks. He was so sick of the Elmire pleasure ground. He doubled up. And Georgie was laughing. And laughing. And Abby put the corned down. He was rolling on the bandstand. I said what is all this about? Abby said you wouldn't know. He said you wouldn't know mama. He said you know them pills you had for Alfred on the windowsill. I put them in yellow's dinner. I said Abby ain't you ashamed. Ain't you ashamed of yourself. I said she had them all day long in the house. That's a shame. Oh he was sick. He was sick. All right. He was sick. I got it. But you see I had them for my boy. And I used to give him two. But God knows how many they put in a man's grub. I don't know. How many they put in his food. They take everything. They take limburger cheese all the skin and all that mess. And they shoved it in chink's tube and smeared it all around. Every time it was playing. He stunk out the golden room over there. Oh chink you stink. And all that poor fella he didn't know when he come home he told me he showed it to me. He wiped it out. He come home and showed it to me said they did that. No, I got a daughter. Oh. Yeah, I got a daughter. And there's seven years difference between them, between Alfred and Alma. Oh. And so, Alfred, he was always sickly, all the time. But then after a long, he got a long time, and then he got diabetes, he got a stroke. And after that, he got the diabetes. And three months before he died, they discovered he had a cancer on the kidney. Oh. But he didn't last. He didn't even live three months. That's what that doing insulin, that insulin, that port-a-main zinc. He got three shots a day. That's how bad he had it. He was most of the time in the hospital in Comas. That's right. In Comas, an insulin shock. Poor fella. He got so towards the last, he used to get convulsions. Oh, Abby's seen him here. In December, and he died that March the 4th, he said, Abby says, oh. He said, Mama, he's all swallowed up. I said, yeah, Abby, I said, he's swallowed up. I said, Abby, he's so scared of diabetes, Abby. Till, I tell you, he's seen Alfred, and then his brother, and Richard has got it. And his mother died with it, and his father and his sister died with it. Now his brother Rudy died with it. Jimmy Kennell. He played cornet too. He played with him too?

I was over, this was around about 1910. Somewhere along around 1910. I was in Biloxi. I had three bands in Biloxi. I had a junior band playing for the junior company. I had one for the West End and one for a volunteer. Three bands. Well, I had all kids. All youngsters ranged in Biloxi, I guess they'd say, from about 16 years down to eight. I had 14 pieces in that band. Mississippi Hook and Ladder was right across the park where we were in, what's the name, Kennedy's Hotel. The park was like here, Kennedy's Hotel there. Mississippi Hook and Ladder was over here, right alongside the park. They had a military band. They played some kind of a tour. I remember that I heard of it. But anyhow, they were running, all the kids, you know, all my bunch of kids was running around Biloxi all that morning. They were all in uniform too. And these soldiers kept us saying that kindergarten band, the kindergarten band, you understand? They were all in uniform. So, all right, we were about to leave to go and meet the parade. The soldier band stood in the middle of the park and they played this piece. I remember now, I knew it. I knew what piece it was. And I got, I lined it up, all the kids, right before Kennedy's Hotel. I made them play Kentucky Days. The gentleman, I swear before Christ, they all took their hats off. All them soldiers took their hats off, you know, and clapped, and clapped, and clapped. They found out there was no kindergarten band. Them kids played music. Oh, Jesus, they played music, you know. And Haley Brunus, and Georgie Brunus, and Merit Brunus, and Abby Brunus, and had Kaz Out. Oh, yeah, Jones Kaz Out. All them kids, you know, brothers, they played music. And I stood right between them and told them how to come down. You played, you played piano, you know. You played mostly ragtime style, didn't you? All ragtime music. All ragtime. All ragtime music. Outside of Maltese, Johnny, in Maltese. Yeah. Outside of Maltese and Maltese, everything was right. They've sort of gotten away from that nowadays. I think the bands, they shouldn't have ragtime bands or jazz bands in the Mardi Gras parades. Instead of these stiff military bands. Yeah. They ought to have that, the spirit. That's right. The spirit is not there from the military march. That's right. No. They've lost that. When we'd be in the Mardi Gras parades, Johnny, three and four bands, you could hear them clapping all along the road. Every time they'd hear our bands play. They used to have Bowler, Red Bowler, Big Red Bowler, he's a military band used to play too. I know him. He used to play military bands. Oh, they used to play that stretch. Yeah. See? And we'd rag it. They'd go for that, like nobody's business. They always did. All they did. Go for that, like nobody's business. Yeah. More music in it. The other is too stiff sounding. That's it. That's it. I can remember. Gentlemen. Well, I couldn't feel the engagements, I'll tell you the Christ's truth. And I had five bands going. I couldn't feel the engagements. I've seen them put off parties and picnics at Millenburg. Till I was able to furnish them a contract. Those were wonderful days, you know. They used to be a lot of people. They used to be a lot of people. They used to be a lot of people. They used to be a lot of people. They used to be a lot of people. They had to build their dear I used to have a coach filled with my men, three, four bands. Them were the days, them were the days.
They played all them halls, the Portuguese and the Washington of Terror, the out- I don't think- All that used to always have ordainances, you know, balls and all.

I don't think there's a hole or a corner in this man's city from Protection River down past St. Bernard that I didn't play. Even played in these lawn dances. Lawn parties, huh? They'd get a top hole and spread it over the ground in the lawn, open, you know. Even played them jobs all along town. Some long parties. These I played in young music. Day and night I was going. Day and night. So you played seven jobs one day? Yes, yes. Yes, indeed. I played, I even advertised that day for antiseptic pills, tablets.
I tell you, and sometimes when they'd catch a carnival that it would be raining. You talk about hard luck drum breaking. Oh, the drum breaking.
She'd be on the job.
Right now they'd split the drum heads.
The minute one of them had their drum heads busted, pass another drum and she'd repair that right now.
You did? I could put the drum heads on. Good.
Yeah. Fix them good. Do you remember some of those pieces that we played on the tape tonight? Do you remember some of those old numbers too?
Yes. That's why I knew the time right away of the music. That's why I told them. She knows the time we used to play. Time right away. Yeah.
It's a shame to say this. Tell them what band plays the same kind of tapestry we played at the same time. What kind of band?
Tell them. Nigga band.
You told me once that George Lewis and Paul Barber and I believe you said.
Yeah, Paul Barber.
Played at the same kind of time. Same kind of time.
There was no difference.
There ain't no difference. Same kind of time.

It's a shame to say it but I tell you. I was at the auditorium the night that Santos played and these other two bands played. But the minute I heard them play I told Alma, I said, that's Papa's music. That's his time and that you could swear it was his band right now. Right now. Yeah.

Right now. Right now. If you didn't see that band, you was away from that band and heard it, you'd say, that's Jack Rains playing there. That's Jack Rains playing there. That's Jack Rains playing there. That's the really is the truth. You mean those tapes, those records you just heard? Yeah. Yeah. Sure. That's Jack Rains playing there. That other band. Right now. Still you'd go in there and see a bunch of niggas. No different. Rather no different. Yeah. Yeah. That's indeed. But I'll tell you the truth.
That is, that is, that there is a shark. And I don't know what kind of music they play. I don't like that.
It ain't because this guy is sitting here that I'm going to.
It's not a long time.
I can't see it.
That's right. It's a different kind of, Johnny plays a different kind of music.
It ain't because he's sitting here that I'm going to say it. But the same, same temperature, same time that he played cornet, all my cornet played it.
Yeah.
Same way. You said it sounded like Richie Brunus.

And then you're my own and all the same. Same way. Ain't no different about it. I never heard nobody play. You're better. I never heard nobody play a cornet time like that. Never. None of them. Almerico, Ossantos, Shockey. Oh, Shockey. Oh. I had Shockey a few times.
I told Dr. Sushaw on that too. I don't like it. I don't like that music. He said, you don't. I said, no, I don't like it, doctor. I don't like it. I don't like that music.

He said, you don't. I said, no, I don't like it, doctor. I don't like it. I said, I don't know what kind of time they play, but I don't like it. I said, I really don't like it. Have you played with Johnny Lala?
Yeah. Did you notice what sort of time he played music in? Well, that's the time we used to play in with Brownlee's band. Johnny Lala too, he played good.
He played good. Yeah. But Johnny, I had one cornet player, was grand.

Then I had another, just that quick, really. I see above the staff, Richie Brunus. Little Vega was the finest trumpet player that was in this man's town. Lawrence Vega. That kid could play a horn. Ragtime? Yeah. Yeah, Lawrence Vega. Brother, that boy, oh, he was young.

He played, that time he played with him and Pacquet and Dave Perkins. Huh. Well, Lawrence Vega played with you. Yeah. And Pacquet and Dave Perkins and you, I forgot who the others were, but anyhow, that's really, and you know Pacquet played good music. Pacquet played good music.
You heard of Ashil Pacquet playing clarinet, haven't you? He played good, he played good.
That's a dark skin.
Yeah. Yeah.
So was Dave Perkins. Married a white girl though. Perkins was fair. Married a white girl. Poikins was fair as a lily and had blue eyes and blonde hair. He had colored blood.
Fair as a lily.
He looked more on a German type or an Irish. He really did. You could never, never think of it.
He was brown skin.

Well, now, Parquet, he was sort of a Mexican type, but not Poikins. Not Poikins. I had one fellow, one of these writers come here one day, and he asked me, he said, Yala Nunes, Yala Nunes was a nigger. I said, oh, no.
I said, no, my friend.

I said, you mistaken. I said, not Yala Nunes, not Alcide Nunes. I said, no, he wasn't. He was a white man. He's a white man. I knew his sisters, his brothers, his father. We went to his father's wake and funeral. And his sister married Louis Morrow. Morrow that had the grocery net out of Millenburg. Big, fat Louis Morrow. I know who he was married. His sister was married to him. And I knew him. He used to play mandolin. He was a little bit of thing like Georgie Brunis, about 10, 12 years old. He was, mm-mm. How did he get that name, Yellow?
Maybe that's why somebody thought that, because they call him Yellow. He was kind of dark.
He was kind of dark. He was kind of dark, yeah. Yeah.
I know them all. Know his brothers. Know his sisters. Know his father. Know his mother.

I told him. I said, no, sir. He ain't. He said, I want to tell you something. I don't know if you'll get in something. I said, well, no. I said, I want to ask you. He said, ain't this Yala Nunes a nigger too? I said, oh, no. I said, no, sir. He's not. Uh-uh. He's not. He ain't.
Anybody would know I would know.
He said, I, he said, well, I heard that. I said, well, you heard wrong. I said, you heard wrong. Whoever told you that don't know him. They might have him mixed up with somebody else. I said.
I guess they got that from his nickname.

Nickname. Yeah, Yala. Yeah, yeah. Yeah. But now, Paki, you could see, you could tell him. You could tell on him too if you looked at him good. He looked like a Mexican. And there was another one too. He had playing with him, Batiste O'Quin. He was too. Oh, yeah.
So I, I, I let him go because I had two already, you know, lined it up and I didn't want any more.
Yeah. He was too. Because he's people and all. Yeah.
He was. And he was a barber and had a white barber shop. Yeah.
He had a white barber shop. Yeah.
He had a white barber shop. No, but there's a. I knew he was, I knew he had copper in his metal.
Let's see. When I have, when I did, if I got that picture.
Did you see, what's the, anything of his name, the drummer with the Dixie Man jazz band when he was in town.
Tony Sparbaro. Tony Sparbaro. Tony Spargo he calls himself now. Tony Sabarbara.
Yeah.
Tony Sabarbara. Did you see him when he was down for Carnival?
No, I wouldn't have ever. He was down for Carnival. Yeah. He was? Yeah. He was? Yeah. He was? Yeah. He was the one, he didn't come down to Chimmy.
He was only here, one, he had to leave the next day.

His mother, I believe, was sick or somebody in the family was sick, so he didn't get to see many people. He left right away. Very short trip. I saw him one day, just for a minute. Gabe, Gabe Pounders' sister is his mother. Who? Gabe Pounders, Tony Sabarbara. Tony Sabarbara. Yeah, I didn't know that. No. Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah. Oh, in Chicago, New York.
Yeah.

I wanted to ask you, did Tom Brown play with you? Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. He's one of the two Teddors. I had Tom and Teddoh playing with me. Yeah. I had five bands Johnny going all the time. Steve Brown played with you too, huh? That's Ted. That's his name. Who? Ted, huh? Ted. Ted. They called him Steve later on. Yeah. Teddoh. Yeah. Teddoh. Uh-huh. Yeah. They called him Steve. Yeah. He was in town recently too. Yeah, I know. I met him. He looked me up. Yeah. He's a wonderful bass player.
There's Merritt. He's good bass player. He's right here. Merritt.
Oh, yeah. There's his coronet. A little short coronet.
Yeah.
Let me see.
Look, and there's George. I don't know why you can't pick up some of those.
That's what we had a band in Crockett. Fireman's over the river. Fireman band. All in red uniforms. And George is the fireman's head on.
Yeah, George.

I was going to ask, what kind of a band did Fisher have? Fisher. Johnny Fisher? Is it a brass band? No, he had an orchestra. Pretty good. It wasn't rag? Pretty good. Pretty good. Chiller used to play with him. Was it ragtime? And this fellow Shannon. This fellow Shannon had with me. He used to play with him too. Fisher had a good band. Was it ragtime? Fisher's band. Ragtime. Yeah. Rag music, yeah. And he used to have, oh, I can't think of his name now. He was on the police a while, playing trombone with him. Fisher. Yeah. Yeah. Not Emile Christian, huh? No, no, no. No. Emile Christian played with you too, didn't he? Yeah.
The three of the Christians. Frank, too. Frank, Emile, and Charlie.

Charlie. You know telling them they used to build them short in those days, didn't they? Yeah, they were funny enough. I was thinking, you know, a lot of people had some beautiful con, silver engraved con cornets. I'd sure like to be able to run across some of those. Must be some of them someplace. They are tucked away somewhere. I'd sure like to find a good one. Throw them all over. You see, all this junk is interesting to look at. It is to me. Anything she's, right away, in a book. Yeah, that's good. Right now. It was left to me. I'd point up a whole lot of stuff when I was, oh, man. Plenty of stuff I'd point up.
I believe, I believe Alfred's Cornet was like that, eh?
A little shark to con, right there?
Alfred's Cornet. Alfred's Cornet. What kind of Cornet was it? B-Flat. B-Flat. Manuel, his brother-in-law been wanting to buy it, but his wife won't, won't part.
The only one playing a knee-flat cornet was Johnny, uh, uh, Dive.
Yeah.
The cuck I dig, of him.
Oh. Uh, Provenzana? Johnny, uh, Provenzana. Provenzana.
Johnny Provenzana. Johnny Provenzana. Oh, mm-hmm. Direct from Italy, a knee-flat.
He was, he was, uh, he used to call us up all the time, poor fella. He was so sick all the time. And he called me off. Okay.
I'm going to say Blottsy, Mississippi. Blottsy, Mississippi. Coych and, uh, West End Hose. Coych and, uh, what's his name, mother?
Hmm? Uh, Gussie Zinneman and, um, uh, what's his name?
Rami Coych?
Um, Martin Coych.
Martin Coych. Martin Coych.
Martin Coych. Yeah, Martin. He's dead and his brother, Robbie, is dead too. And now, Gussie Zinneman ain't dead, is he?
No, Gussie's dead and his brother. He plays cornet and, uh...

Clarinet. And clarinet. That's, uh, that's Zinneman. That's Coych, Martin Coych. He was good too. That's the, that was in Alexander, Louisiana there. Yeah, that's an old, I got another picture of that. Sitting on the piano or something? That other picture, that other move.

Maybe. No, no, it's a couch. No, I thought it was a chair. I thought it was a piano stool. Yeah, that's a couch. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. You got more trash than this stuff here in the house, Lord. This is good. No trash. Look, here's a... Here's some more. There's some more. Here's some more. Here's some more.
Here's some more.
Here's some more. Here's some more.
Here's yellow. There's yellow Nunes. There's Eddie Edwards and Tony and La Rocca. Yeah, Eddie Edwards. And La Rocca. Yeah. That's yellow. Yellow Nunes. And that's Regis.
He playing that. That's the Dixieland Jazz Band.
Yeah.
That's yellow Nunes. The Shields was with them later. I thought the... Yeah. That's not Shields though, is it? No. No. No. That's yellow. The first Dixieland Jazz Band before Shields went with them.
Yeah. Yeah.
Uh-huh.
Yeah.
And this... Yeah, right here.

It has his name and sign there. Yeah, A. Nunes. He sent us that picture. Yeah. The first band, not WWL, but WLW. Remember? That before WWL? Yeah. The first band went in on the air. That's them. That's... That's Mallow. That's one of the Mallows. And that's Bud Loyer Canna. That's Emile Q. That's my son. And... One of them is Cousins and the other one is Trabbe K. I don't... This fella is dead too. And he's dead. And he's dead.
The banjo and the drum and the sax is dead.
Yes. And my son is dead. And this is Emile Q. I don't know if Emile Q is dead or not. I couldn't say.
I couldn't say myself.
No, but that he had...
Well, they must be all old men now. I don't know. If they're living, I don't know.
These fellas worked in the Maison Blanche. But this is Bud Loyer Canna. You see? Bud played tuba too? Yes.
I never knew Bud played tuba. Yes.
We bought a tuba for Buddy.
We took him off a bass bit and put him on tuba.
I never knew that.

I've never seen that original Dixieland band before. No. What was the Nunez's name? I can't read from... It's A. Nunez here. Alcide is his name. I couldn't see whether there's another word there from... Something up of... C-O-Z. C-O-Z. C-O-Z. Maybe. Oh, C-O-Z. Maybe.
Maybe. Maybe. He called himself C-O-Z. C-O-Z. He called himself C-O-Z.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. C-O-Z A. Nunez.
Yeah.
That's a good picture.
I've never seen him. Yeah, it's a good picture of him, I mean. Yeah, it is. Yeah. Like me. Yeah, it's a good picture of him. Yeah, he sent us that. He sent us that.
He sent us. And who was that piano player I wanted?
Regus. I don't know. That's Regus. That's Regus. Yeah. I don't know him. Yeah. I don't know all these. I know them except him. I don't know Regus.

This is one of the finest trombone players I ever heard. You're wrong. Yeah. You're wrong. Who's the finest? Uh, Humpback Daly, they could give them all chords and spades and beat them out. Yeah. Really? I never heard him. Jesus Christ, Humpback Daly. Oh, he was good.
He was good.
Val or Slide, either. Val or Slide. Yeah, he was good.
He was good. He was good.

Give them all chords and spades and beat them out. Yeah. And Perkins was a trombone player but Perkins couldn't hold a trombone player alongside Humpback Gallaty, Bill Gallaty. Bill Gallaty. Oh, that's the father of the present trumpet player.
Bill Gallaty. He's playing trumpet, his son?
He played the mount harp too, don't he? His son. I never knew that, didn't he? I'm his godfather. Yeah? Yeah.
Mm-hmm.
The young fella, huh? Yeah.
His first, um...
Well, the old man was a fine trombone player. Oh!
Yeah, yeah. Right. He was.
Brother, he'd make it sing.
He was good.
You know, you ought to hear Emile Christian now. Oh, Emile plays a good trombone. They tell me. I don't know. I mean to tell you, he is terrific now. Is he?
I thought he couldn't play no more.
He's ten times better than he ever was. I spoke to him Monday.
He got his teeth out.

They won't hire him because he's an old man, you see? But I played with him. You know that, uh, you know that time you, uh... I see. You know that time I said that Brunus boy hired us for across the river? Yeah. I got Emile. I've been recording with Emile, too.
Yeah. Emile is, I tell you, he's... Emile is about 64 years old.
He's older than that, isn't he?
No. Mm-mm. He's one year older than my son. They work together at the Postal Telegraph and everything else.
Yeah. I spoke to him Monday.
Yeah. Yeah, I spoke to him Monday, yeah. Emile Christian. They're living right next to us. He was a good friend, I'll tell you. Oh, I tell you.
You should have heard him that day we played across the river, Emile.
Emile. But I tell you, he really aged, though, didn't he? That's the total.

Yeah, he looks old, but he played that trombone like a 25-year-old boy that day. He was a good trombone player, though, Hank. His brother was a good one, too, but... I'm telling you, he played some licks that would have been hard to play on trumpet. Yeah. And I mean, he just executed them perfectly. They weren't any corny licks. They were good. Clear. Every note in them were... Every note was well selected. You know, clever. Clear, yeah. Oh, I mean...
Well, he stopped playing on the kind of his teeth. No. No?
He got some false teeth specially made for that. Oh, he's got them. And I'm telling you, he plays better on those false teeth than he ever played in his life.
Oh, no kidding. I thought you couldn't play with false teeth.
He's got two sets of them. One for eating and one for playing. Oh, I never thought that...
I broke some money in the baker shop.
Yeah?
When I come from the doctor.

Yeah? I guess he's disgusted because, you know, he's old and they won't hire him. Oh. You see? Yeah. And he's wonderful. Ain't that something? He's wonderful. I got him on those, you know, those Mardi Gras records I made, the If Ever I Cease to Love, and King Zulu Parade, and those records. Yeah. And oh, he's just wonderful. Let me tell you a little story, Johnny. He was good.
I know he was.

Let me tell you a little story about the Chinamen. I had them on bass pedal and had them on guitar all the time, you know. And it seemed like I needed more tuba players. I only had two at the time, you understand? Then I got Lawyer Cannon, May Street, and I had to get five tuba players anyway. So, here comes young Buffalo Bill, a fellow by the name O'Brien, for the Wild West Show. Well, they found out about me, you understand? They come down to shame me. And I had Cascaro on tuba. Cascaro took Deathly Sick. He died shortly after that, too. I believe it was Poison. So, here I had this job. And that show was in the lot on Espinade between the river and Decatur, on the downtown side of the street. Great big tent show, Wild West Show. Cascaro sent my word, impossible. Couldn't play. Jesus, I said, what am I going to do now? Had all the other players engaged, playing their jobs. What did I do? I go to Cascaro's house and get these tuba. Called the gentleman, you come on out here. Now get in this band. Here, play this. The gentleman said, what the hell do I know about that? The kids, you know, I don't know nothing about that. Shove that in your face and play it.
All right, he said.

All right, he said. If you say so, it's all right. We stood by number nine, Jane Jane House, on Decatur and Espinade. I lined them all around the circle. Said to the Chinaman, I said, whenever you can catch time, the Chinaman, that you can fill up a note, put it in there. This baritone, I said, hold up as much as possible for you. All right. Put the tuba in the Chinaman's hand. Every night we played for two weeks. Every night for two weeks. Chinaman on the tube. Start to put them in parades. Start to moat around. Said to that, that Chinaman played a tuba. I went to Cascro, the old lady, his mother, and I bought the tuba. Eight dollars. Eight dollars. Eight dollars. Eight dollars. I'll give it to the Charmin. Ever since that, the chick was playing. No more bass, middle guitar. Tuba. You sure picked a good one, too. Yeah. Now, the same way you take La Rocca. Nick, Nick come down a couple of times in my rehearsal, you know. And, uh, he'd sit around listening, you know, one thing or another. And, uh, bring down his cornet and he'd listen around there, you know. And the first thing you know, I got through that much work, Johnny, that I put him in the band anyhow to fill out. To fill out. Go along, go along. Even over at Elmire Pleasure Ground. Over at, uh, at, uh, Algier Park. All around there, I had every Saturday and Sunday. Cramer's lot. Three or four of them places over there. Had them on Saturdays and Sundays. La Rocca used to come and sit on Saturdays and Sunday. segments.title: Laine's trap drum beat returns after 40 years; Fisher's band and the Stevens drummers
segments.summary: Reacting to the tape just played, Laine and Wiggs discuss how his cymbal beat came back after 40 years. Laine recalls Happy Schilling recognizing his bass drum and Johnny Fisher's offer, filled with the Stevens drummers.

segments.title: Taking over the military band as major, Spanish-American War era
segments.summary: Laine tells how Major Violet asked him to lead a 35-man military band, which he enlarged with piccolos and drilled for street marches until they were to ship out.

segments.title: Looking at an 1896 photo; Laine's fancy uniform
segments.summary: They find a faded 1896 photo of the band, and Laine says he refused the heavily decorated uniform the major offered.

segments.title: Identifying the Brunies brothers in a photograph
segments.summary: Wiggs, Laine and Blanche pick out Georgie, Abbie, Richard, Henny and Rudy Brunies, Harry Shannon and Bud Lyakana in a photo.

segments.title: Copies of the photo for the Brunies boys; how Laine paid them
segments.summary: Blanche explains getting copies made for Merritt, Abbie and Georgie, estimating Georgie's age, and Laine says how he paid the boys, mothers getting the money.

segments.title: Scrapbook pictures: Alexandria 1917 band, gold record, Chink Martin
segments.summary: Scrapbook photos of the 1917 Alexandria job, the gold record presentation and a Gretna parade with Chink Martin on tuba.

segments.title: Wiggs's pictures and his father
segments.summary: Short scrapbook chatter, ending with Wiggs's photo of his father, a doctor.

segments.title: Brunies reunion visit at the Laine house and photos in the yard
segments.summary: Blanche describes the day Georgie, Abbie and Merritt visited, shows yard photos, and Rudy Brunies's son Henny; Wiggs says that nephew booked him across the river and followed his band.

segments.title: Blanche's memories of the Brunies boys' pranks and Johnny Lala
segments.summary: Blanche recalls the boys sleeping at her house, Johnny Lala staying over, and Abbie and Georgie's mischief, Chink Martin's tuba smeared with cheese, and pills in a player's dinner.

segments.title: Freddie Williams thrown out for beating Georgie
segments.summary: Laine asks about Freddie Williams, and Blanche explains why she put him out of the house for attacking Georgie Brunies.

segments.title: Drinks, and Laine running three bands of unruly kids
segments.summary: After a pause for refreshments, Laine says he had three bands on the street at once, and the boys misbehaved whenever his back was turned.

segments.title: Blanche's son Alfred and his illness; Abbie's fear of diabetes
segments.summary: Raymond Burke is remembered at Alfred's wake, and Blanche tells of Alfred's sickly life, diabetes, stroke and death, and Abbie Brunies's fear of the disease.

segments.title: Jimmy Kennell and a week of seven jobs
segments.summary: Brief talk about the seven jobs in a day and cornetist Jimmy Kennell.

segments.title: Kindergarten band in Biloxi and the lost spirit of Mardi Gras bands
segments.summary: Around 1910 Laine's band of kids in Biloxi plays Kentucky Days and wins over a soldier band; he then says ragtime bands beat stiff military bands in parades and he ran up to five bands.

segments.title: Playing seven jobs a day all over New Orleans; drum heads
segments.summary: Laine says he played every corner of the city, lawn parties and halls, seven jobs a day, and recalls splitting drum heads in the rain and repairing them.

segments.title: The old-time beat and the Black bands that played the same time
segments.summary: They compare the tape's time to the music of George Lewis's band and others, Laine and Blanche saying the Black bands played just like his.

segments.title: Comparing later cornet players; Lawrence Vega, Pacquet and Perkins
segments.summary: Laine praises his cornet players, saying none played the time like them; he singles out Lawrence Vega, with Pacquet and Dave Perkins.

segments.title: Pacquet and Dave Perkins and their ancestry
segments.summary: They discuss the skin colour and background of Achille Pacquet and Dave Perkins.

segments.title: Defending Alcide 'Yellow' Nunez as white
segments.summary: Blanche tells how she corrected a writer who thought Yellow Nunez was Black, citing his family, and Laine suggests the nickname caused it.

segments.title: Tony Sbarbaro's visit to New Orleans
segments.summary: Wiggs asks if Laine saw drummer Tony Sbarbaro, who made a short carnival trip; his mother was Gabe Pounders's sister.

segments.title: Tom and Steve Brown, the Fireman's band and Johnny Fisher's orchestra
segments.summary: Laine confirms Tom Brown and Steve Brown played with him, mentions Merritt and Georgie in the firemen's band, and describes Fisher's ragtime orchestra and the Christian brothers.

segments.title: Old cornets, Alfred's cornet, Johnny Provenzana
segments.summary: They talk about old silver cornets, Alfred's B-flat cornet, and Johnny Provenzana, who played an E-flat cornet, plus Biloxi musicians.

segments.title: Coych and Zinneman, Alexandria photo
segments.summary: Naming Martin Coych, Gussie Zinneman and brothers, and an Alexandria photo.

segments.title: Photo of the first Dixieland Jazz Band and Yellow Nunez's signed picture
segments.summary: Looking at a photo of the early band with Nunez, Eddie Edwards and La Rocca, and a WLW radio band with Blanche's son and Bud Loyacano.

segments.title: Humpback Daly and Bill Gallaty, great trombonists
segments.summary: Laine rates Humpback Daly and Bill Gallaty as the best trombonists, noting Gallaty's son plays trumpet.

segments.title: Emile Christian's trombone playing today
segments.summary: Wiggs says Emile Christian plays better than ever with false teeth, recorded on his Mardi Gras records, and Blanche notes he lives next door.

segments.title: Teaching Chink Martin tuba, and La Rocca sitting in
segments.summary: Laine tells how he put Chink Martin on tuba for a Wild West show when Cascaro fell sick, and how Nick La Rocca began sitting in with his band.
